newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies new trial for Oklahoma City bomber.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies new trial for Oklahoma City bomber.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case on Monday denied Timothy McVeigh's request for a new trial and said he would impose a death sentence on the Gulf War veteran on Thursday.
McVeigh was convicted and sentenced to death by a jury in June for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people.

McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols is scheduled to go on trial on Sept. 29 in Denver. But his attorneys on Monday filed for a change of venue based on heavy media coverage of the first trial in the Denver area, the attorneys said without elaboration. But a source said Nichols' lawyers said they want the case moved to San Francisco.
McVeigh was found guilty of the bombing on June 2 and the same jury on June 13 sentenced him to die. He is being held in a suburban Denver federal prison.

In a written order, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch said: "All of the questions and issues raised in the defendant's motion have been considered and ruled on in the course of pre-trial proceedings and during the trial, and the court adheres to those rulings."
Prosecutors had opposed granting a new trial, arguing that McVeigh's was "close to perfect."
Requests for new trials are often filed, but seldom granted. The judge's order said that McVeigh is to appear on Thursday morning for his formal sentencing.

The judge's refusal to grant a new trial paves the way for appealing McVeigh's conviction. "I'm not surprised," McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones said, referring to the judge's decision not to grant a new trial.
Jones said McVeigh had been informed of the decision.

McVeigh asked for a new trial based on 13 grounds including a juror's alleged remark during the trial, immense pre-trial publicity and emotional testimony by survivors and relatives of people who died in the bombing.

One juror is alleged to have said "I think we all know what the verdict should be." Jones had wanted the judge to hold a hearing to determine if the jurors had been improperly influenced by the comment.
But the judge refused, saying he believed the remark had been made in jest.

The appeal will also be based on the judge's refusal to hear testimony from a government informant who would have testitifed that she had told federal authorities that white supremacists in eastern Oklahoma had talked about bombing federal buildings.
The judge's refusal to delay the start of the trial after published reports of a purported confession by McVeigh will be another issue in McVeigh's appeal.
